primary_meaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, to 'sanctify' means to set apart as holy for God, and 'sanctification' denotes the process (and in some texts the accomplished state) by which believers are made holy — separated from sin and common use, consecrated to God, and progressively conformed to the moral character of Christ through the work of the Holy Spirit. The dominant systematic formulation, especially in Protestant theology, treats sanctification as the ongoing transformation of the believer's life that follows and is distinct from justification, culminating in glorification.
primary_basis: Leviticus 11:44-45 ('Be holy, for I am holy')
Exodus 19:5-6 (Israel set apart as a holy nation)
John 17:17-19 ('Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth')
1 Thessalonians 4:3 ('This is the will of God, your sanctification')
1 Thessalonians 5:23 ('May the God of peace himself sanctify you completely')
Romans 6:19-22 (slaves of righteousness leading to sanctification)
1 Corinthians 1:2 and 1 Corinthians 6:11 ('sanctified in Christ Jesus... you were washed, you were sanctified')
2 Thessalonians 2:13 ('salvation through sanctification by the Spirit')
Hebrews 10:10, 10:14 (sanctified through the offering of Christ's body once for all)
Hebrews 12:14 ('the holiness without which no one will see the Lord')
1 Peter 1:15-16 ('be holy in all your conduct')
Romans 8:29 (conformed to the image of his Son, often cited for the goal of sanctification)

alternatives.meaning: Progressive sanctification: a lifelong, gradual moral and spiritual growth in holiness after conversion, cooperative between the Spirit and the believer, never complete in this life. This is the classic Reformed/Lutheran/broadly evangelical framing.

Definitive or positional sanctification: a once-for-all setting apart of the believer at conversion, so that Christians are already 'saints' and 'sanctified' regardless of moral progress. Often held alongside, not instead of, progressive sanctification (emphasized by John Murray and much New Testament scholarship on Paul's usage).

Entire sanctification / Christian perfection: a distinct post-conversion work of grace in which the believer is cleansed from inward sin and enabled to love God perfectly in this life (Wesleyan, Methodist, Holiness, and some Pentecostal traditions).

Sanctification as infusion of sanctifying grace or deification (theosis): in Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox theology, sanctification is not sharply separated from justification but is an ongoing participation in divine life mediated through grace and the sacraments, aimed at union with God.

Cultic/ceremonial consecration: in the Old Testament and some New Testament usage, 'sanctify' simply means to dedicate persons, objects, places, or times (priests, vessels, the tabernacle, the Sabbath) to sacred use, without implying inner moral transformation. Scholars treat this as the root sense from which the moral-spiritual meaning developed.
basis: 1 Timothy 4:4-5 (food sanctified by word and prayer)

alternatives.meaning: Sanctifying God / hallowing his name: a reverse usage in which humans (or God himself) 'sanctify' God's name by honoring it as holy or vindicating it, rather than God sanctifying people.

notes: The core lexical meaning — 'to make or declare holy; to set apart for God' (Hebrew qadash, Greek hagiazo) — is essentially undisputed across traditions and academic scholarship. The recognizable disagreements concern the theology and mechanics of sanctification (progressive vs. definitive vs. entire vs. sacramental/theosis models), not the basic meaning of the term. Because the term is more a doctrinal-lexical concept than a symbol, 'symbolic meaning' here is best understood as its theological sense; there is settled consensus on that sense even though denominations divide over how sanctification occurs and whether it can be completed in this life.
